items.title: Trump urges calls to Arkansas senator in push for permanent daylight saving time
items.content_html:
President appeared to share phone number of Tom Cotton for people to call to push him to support measure

Donald Trump on Saturday put pressure on the US senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of his fellow Republican and the chair of the Senate intelligence committee.

The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including the president and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.

items.title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes
items.content_html:
With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia

Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.

But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. items.title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over

items.content_html: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

items.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them

items.title: Women's Basketball World Cup: Can Germany harness a boom?
items.content_html: Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.

items.title: Africa's richest man Dangote's IPO out of reach in Nigeria

items.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
items.content_html: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade.

items.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
items.content_html: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the event of a crisis.

items.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
items.content_html: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

items.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes
items.content_html: The Goethe-Institut was one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. However, following Moscow's decision to close its offices, all employees will have to stop working by September 13.

items.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations

items.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace

items.content_html: The PISA 2025 results reveal record-low student performance, with digital distractions and AI use raising concerns. Germany is faring worse than ever.

items.content_html: As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.
